title: About
text: I am a social sciences researcher specializing in the analysis of the dynamics of nation-building and their long-term effects on ethnic group relations, conflict, and socio-political change. My work offers a comparative perspective on the consequences of Western (e.g., British, French) and non-Western (Ottoman Empire) models of nation- and empire-building. By integrating Geographic Information System (GIS) tools, quantitative methods, and archival research with traditional qualitative analysis, I employ innovative methodologies to advance historical and comparative studies. I hold a PhD from McGill University, where my research and teaching earned multiple awards for excellence, and a Master’s degree from the University of Oxford. Currently, I serve as a Juan de la Cierva Postdoctoral Fellow at the Institut Barcelona d’Estudis Internacionals (IBEI) and am a Postdoctoral Researcher for the ERC-funded ETHNICGOODS project. Currently, I am working on a series of collaborative research articles that explore topics such as cultural elimination, language grievances and ethnic conflict, and the pitfalls of anachronism in social science.

I am a mixed-methods social sciences researcher and educator whose work critically advances the understanding of nationalism, ethnic conflict, and imperialism. My contributions intersect three core areas: the re-examination of nationalism as a transformative and often contingent phenomenon; the integration of innovative methodologies—including Geographic Information System (GIS) tools and advanced quantitative techniques—into sociological and historical analysis; and theoretical advancements that challenge and refine dominant frameworks in sociology and related disciplines. My research engages with pressing debates on the legacies of imperialism, the role of historical education systems in shaping identity, and the mechanisms by which conflict and transformation affect socio-political cohesion.

title: Teaching
text:
Winter 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 · Master’s Elective · 4 Credits · IBEI
Instructor for a master-level elective exploring how history shapes contemporary global outcomes. The course bridges comparative historical methods with pressing substantive questions, structured around four thematic pillars: colonialism & capitalism, human-environment interactions, fascism, and conflict.
Rather than treating history as mere background, the course trains students to interrogate the mechanisms through which the past persists — drawing on path dependence, critical junctures, and comparative methods. A distinctive feature of the 2026 edition is the AI Historiography Audit (40% of the grade): students generate AI-produced historical essays and audit them against primary sources and course readings, developing skills to identify factual hallucinations, interpretive bias, and theoretical superficiality in algorithmically generated text.
Themes covered: Historical causation & temporality · Case selection & comparative methods · Sugar, slavery & global capitalism · Decolonization & neo-imperialism · Climate politics & landscapes · The origins and contemporary mutations of fascism · The Palestinian-Israeli conflict

Substitute instructor for a 200-level introductory course on sociology. The course focuses on the mechanisms by which educational institutions foster and maintain equalities and inequalities around the world.







Summer 2019, Fall 2021
Instructor for a 200-level introductory course on sociology. The course introduced students to a wide range of topics including (but not limited to) social inequality and social class, race and ethnicity, gender, deviance and social movements.







Winter 2018, 2021
Instructor for a 200-level introductory course on sociology of global development.
